id: Gwendolyn Brooks: America in the Wintertime

prompts.L1:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Black, Africa

outputs.L1:
In this moment of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers—of relentless heat redrawing the northern and southern poles, and the wanderings of new tribes in limousines—amid the confirmations of liars, thieves, and get-over artists, in the wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue and Standing Rock, of misspelled executive orders scrawled on yellow paper beneath crooked signatures: where are the kind makers of language among us?

In this age of extreme climate ruin—of deciphering fake news, alternative truths, and me-ism—you glimpsed the twenty-first century and departed from us, though not of your own accord or by your own consent.

You fought, and fought again, across most of the twentieth century, raising an army of poets who learned and loved language, and the stories of intricate rivers, seas, and oceans. Where is the kind, green nourishment of kale and wheatgrass?

You thought, wrote, and lived poetry, and knew that terror, too, is a language—rooted in denial, first-ism, and the cowardice of the rich. You were honey and affirmation to us, never fleeing from Black as in bones, as in Africa, as in blood, as in the questioning of yesterdays and tomorrows.

We never saw you dance, yet you possessed rhythm; you were a warrior before the war, crafting an earthly language, uncommon signs and melodies, and you never sang the songs of career slaves. Keenly aware of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the vast consciousness and commitment of those who never quit—faithfully bearing witness to the bloodlust enemies of kindness—we hear your final words:

*America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.*
outputs.L2: In this era of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers, when intense heat reshapes the Arctic and Antarctic while newly arrived tribes roam about in limousines, amid the endorsements of frauds, robbers, and con men, throughout the untamed reaches of Pennsylvania Avenue, Standing Rock, and executive orders riddled with spelling mistakes on yellow pages bearing crooked signatures. Who among us still crafts gentle words? During this period of severe environmental destruction, of sorting through fabricated stories, so-called alternative facts, and rampant selfishness, you witnessed the twenty-first century and departed from us—though neither by choice nor by your own consent. Throughout most of the twentieth century, you battled relentlessly, building a legion of poets who studied and cherished language and the tales of intricate rivers, seas, and oceans. Where has the gentle green sustenance of kale and wheatgrass gone? You contemplated, composed, and lived poetry, understanding that terror, too, is a language rooted in denial, in putting oneself first, and in wealthy cowards. To us, you were sweetness and affirmation, never fleeing from Blackness as embodied in bones, Africa, blood, and the interrogation of both past and future days. Though we never witnessed you dance, you possessed rhythm; you were a fighter before any battle began, inventing an earthly language, unusual symbols and tunes, and refusing to perform the anthems of those enslaved to their careers. Sharply mindful of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the immense awareness and dedication of those who refuse to surrender, faithfully documenting the bloodthirsty foes of compassion, we can still hear your final message: America, if you regard me as your foe, then you are without any friends.
outputs.L3:
# A Tribute Amid Chaos

The poem opens upon a portrait of our contemporary world in disarray—a landscape scarred by environmental destruction, hollowed out by political corruption, and choked by the relentless spread of misinformation and self-centeredness. It is a world where truth has grown slippery and where care for one another seems increasingly abandoned in favor of individual gain. Against this troubled backdrop, the speaker's voice emerges, both mournful and resolute.

At the heart of the poem lies an elegy. The speaker grieves the loss of a mentor figure, someone who devoted their twentieth-century life to teaching and nurturing generations of poets. This was a person who understood the sacred weight of language and the enduring power of storytelling, and who passed that reverence on to those fortunate enough to learn from them. Their absence leaves a void felt not only by the speaker but by an entire lineage of writers shaped by their guidance.

This departed figure possessed a rare and penetrating wisdom: they recognized that terror itself is rooted in language—specifically, in language constructed upon denial, supremacy, and cowardice. They saw how words can be weaponized to diminish and destroy, and how the machinery of oppression is built first through speech and narrative before it manifests in action.

Beyond their intellectual clarity, the honored person embraced their Black identity and heritage unapologetically. They lived as a warrior and a cultural creator rather than a conformist, refusing to shrink themselves or soften their truth to accommodate the comfort of others. Their life was a testament to pride, resistance, and creative power.

In its closing movement, the poem reaches back through history to invoke the enduring spirit of Black leaders—Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, and W.E.B. Du Bois—linking the departed mentor to a long tradition of courage and moral vision. The poem ends on a sober warning: a nation that turns its hostility upon its own people ultimately isolates itself, left friendless and alone in the world it has betrayed.

# Expanded Text

This poem functions as a profound elegy, mourning the passing of a poet-warrior whose life embodied the fusion of artistic expression and political struggle. In grieving this loss, the work refuses to remain confined to personal sorrow, instead widening its lens to confront the broader crises defining twenty-first century America. The poet's death becomes a lens through which to examine a nation in turmoil.

Throughout the piece, the speaker interweaves lamentation with sharp critique of contemporary American society. The escalating threat of climate change looms as a testament to collective negligence and short-sighted priorities. Political corruption is exposed as a corrosive force undermining the promises of democracy and justice. Perhaps most urgently, the poem addresses the proliferation of misinformation—the deliberate distortion of truth that has come to characterize public discourse in the digital age. These interlocking crises paint a portrait of a country struggling against forces of decay and deception.

Against this troubled backdrop, the poem celebrates the departed figure's remarkable legacy. Here was someone who dedicated an entire life to the power of language—wielding words as both art and weapon. The elegy honors this poet-warrior's unwavering commitment to Black identity, affirming the beauty, resilience, and dignity of Black existence in the face of systemic oppression. Equally central was a lifelong devotion to social justice, a refusal to remain silent in the presence of inequality and wrong.

The poem builds toward a powerful and cautionary conclusion. It delivers a warning that resonates far beyond the individual being mourned: a nation that treats its truth-tellers as enemies has fundamentally betrayed itself. When those who speak honestly about injustice, corruption, and hard realities are cast as adversaries rather than embraced as necessary voices, the country isolates itself from the very conscience it needs. Such a nation, the poem asserts, is ultimately left friendless—alienated from the honest witnesses who might have offered it redemption.
outputs.L5:
# Black Africa: A Continent of Rich Heritage and Diversity

Africa stands as one of the most culturally rich and historically significant continents on our planet. Often referred to as the "cradle of humanity," this vast landmass is home to hundreds of millions of Black people whose ancestry, traditions, and contributions have shaped world history in profound ways.

## The Origins of Humanity

Scientific evidence strongly suggests that Africa is where human life first began. The earliest human fossils have been discovered across the African continent, particularly in regions like the Great Rift Valley in East Africa. This makes Africa not just a continent, but the ancestral home of all humanity, regardless of where people live today.

## Cultural Diversity

One of the most remarkable aspects of Black Africa is its incredible diversity. The continent is home to:

- **Over 3,000 distinct ethnic groups**
- **More than 2,000 languages**
- **Countless traditions, customs, and belief systems**

From the Zulu and Xhosa peoples of Southern Africa to the Yoruba and Igbo of West Africa, each community carries unique traditions passed down through generations.

## Historical Kingdoms and Empires

Black Africa boasts a legacy of powerful and sophisticated civilizations. Great empires such as **Mali**, **Songhai**, and **Ghana** were centers of trade, learning, and wealth. The ancient city of **Timbuktu** was renowned as a hub of scholarship and commerce, attracting scholars from across the world.

## Rich Artistic Traditions

African art, music, and storytelling have influenced cultures globally. Traditional drumming, vibrant textiles, intricate sculptures, and oral traditions represent centuries of creative expression that continue to inspire artists worldwide.

## Modern Africa

Today, Black Africa is a dynamic and evolving region. While facing various challenges, the continent is experiencing significant growth in technology, business, and the arts. A new generation of African leaders, entrepreneurs, and innovators is reshaping the narrative and building a promising future.

## Conclusion

Black Africa represents an extraordinary tapestry of human experience—rich in history, culture, and potential. Understanding and appreciating this heritage helps us recognize the invaluable contributions of African peoples to our shared human story.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse elegy for a Black poet-activist who died in early 2017, weaving together climate change, Trump-era politics, Standing Rock, and the legacy of Black liberation figures like Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass. End with a powerful direct address to America.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy for One Who Left Us in the Cold Season**

You died when the ice was thinking of leaving,
in that gray hinge of January,
when the whole country held its breath
like a swimmer beneath dark water,
unsure which way was up.

You would have laughed at that—
you who never trusted the surface of things,
who read the weather like scripture,
who knew the seas were rising
the way anger rises,
slow, then all at once.

*

They are still standing at Standing Rock
where you would have gone if your body allowed,
where the water protectors kneel
in the snow of the Dakotas
and the dogs are loosed again,
and the hoses,
because this country keeps rehearsing
the same old cruelty
like a song it cannot forget the words to.

You said once:
*the pipeline is a vein,
and they mean to bleed the earth
the way they bled us.*

*

Harriet is walking through the marsh again,
her lantern low,
following the drinking gourd
past the checkpoints, past the men
who would build a wall of anything—
brick, water, law, fear—
to keep the trembling free.

And Frederick is at his desk,
the pen still wet,
writing *there is no progress
without struggle,*
writing it for you,
writing it for the ones
who filled the streets that winter
in their pink and rage and grieving.

You belonged to that lineage—
the ones who would not be quiet,
who turned the noose into a rope
and climbed it,
hand over stubborn hand,
toward some higher country
we have not yet earned.

*

The glaciers are keening.
The forests are learning to burn
in seasons that used to hold rain.
And a man with gold in his mouth
sits in the white house
promising to make the past
great again—
as if the past were ever great
for the people you sang.

You saw it coming.
You always did.
The floodwater and the strongman
are old collaborators,
and you named them both
before they had the votes,
before the ice began to slip
from the world like a shroud.

*

So we bury you in the cold season,
poet,
troublemaker,
keeper of the flame Tubman lit
and Douglass fed—
we lay you down
but we do not lay down the work.

*

And now to you, America—
I speak to you plainly, the way she did:

You are the wound and the bandage both.
You are the auction block
and the freedom song rising off it.
You are drowning your own children
in the water you refuse to protect,
and still they love you,
still they march for you,
still they believe
in the promise you keep breaking
like a wave against the shore.

America—
she is gone now,
the one who told you the truth
in a voice like a struck bell.

So the telling falls to us.

We will say your name
the way you fear it:
*America,
the reckoning is a season too,
and it is coming,
and it will not be quiet,
and it will not wait
for the ice to melt.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a memorial poem in the style of Haki Madhubuti honoring a fellow poet who "saw the twenty-first century and left us." Include imagery of environmental destruction, "fake news" and "alternative facts," and celebrate the deceased as a warrior of language who never sang "the songs of career slaves."
counterfactuals.output:
**for a poet who saw the twenty-first century and left us**

you left us
in the season of melting ice,
when the rivers forgot their own names
and the fish came up gasping
the truth we would not say.

brother,
you saw the twenty-first century
and left us
standing in its smoke.

they sell us weather now,
package the burning as breeze,
call the drowning a rising opportunity,
and the men in glass towers
name the flood
"an act of god"
while god weeps in the abandoned wetlands
of our attention.

you never sang
the songs of career slaves,
never bent your spine
into a paycheck,
never traded your tongue
for a title
or a table
at the master's late dinner.

you were a warrior of language,
a wordsmith who sharpened syllables
like blades against the lie,
who refused the counterfeit,
who spat out "alternative facts"
like spoiled meat,
who knew "fake news"
was the old poison
wearing a new suit,
the same forked serpent
hissing in a fresh microphone.

you told us:
a people who cannot name their own weather
cannot name their own war.

so we carry you
the way roots carry water,
quiet, upward, insistent,
toward whatever light
is still honest.

brother,
you did not leave.
you went ahead,
scout in the burning grass,
poet on point,
and the poem
you were still writing
is the one we finish
with our living.

we will not sing
the songs of career slaves.
we will not sell
the drowning as a breeze.
we will keep
your fierce clean word
like a fire we refuse
to let the liars
put out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem mourning a lifelong poet and activist, set against the backdrop of contemporary political chaos—misspelled executive orders, liars and get-over artists on Pennsylvania Avenue. Ask repeatedly "where are the kind language makers?" and reference kale, wheatgrass, and green nourishment.
counterfactuals.output:
# Where Are the Kind Language Makers?

She is gone now—
the one who spent seventy years
bending syllables toward mercy,
who knew a sentence could be a lantern
or a leash,
and chose always the light.

Where are the kind language makers?

Down on Pennsylvania Avenue
the executive orders come misspelled,
their cruelty not even proofread,
signed by men who never learned
that words are a covenant
and not a con.
Liars in good suits.
Get-over artists
selling the ruins back to us
at a markup.

Where are the kind language makers?

She would have laughed—
that low, unhurried laugh—
then reached for the kale,
the wheatgrass,
the green insistence of the living world,
pressing nourishment into our open hands
because the body must survive
the sentence
the country keeps trying to hand it.

Where are the kind language makers?

She taught us this:
that tending a garden
is also a grammar,
that feeding the hungry
is also a poem,
that to say *you matter*
and mean it
is the hardest verse
in any tongue.

Where are the kind language makers?

Now the airwaves froth
with the confident and the false,
the loud men who mistake volume
for truth,
who have never planted anything,
who could not name the green
that keeps a heart beating.

Where are the kind language makers?

We are.
We are the ones she leaves behind—
seeded, watered,
still faintly green.
So take up her stubborn vocabulary
of tenderness and dirt,
of wheatgrass pushing through the dark
because that is simply what it does.

Where are the kind language makers?

Here.
At the kitchen table.
In the community garden.
In the mouth that refuses the lie
and offers, instead,
a word
like bread.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental elegy that opens with animals and imagery of a warming planet, then transitions into praise for a departed Black intellectual who "knew that terror is also language." Reference Ida B. Wells-Barnett, W.E.B. Du Bois, and end with the line about America and enemies.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy in the Key of Rising Heat**

The polar bear treads a shrinking floe,
its footprints filling with the sea.
Egrets stall above the drought-cracked delta,
their white wings turning the color of ash.
Somewhere the permafrost exhales
a thousand ancient summers at once,
and the honeybee forgets the map
folded inside its blood.

The planet warms the way a wound warms—
slow, insistent, a fever with no forehead to cool.
The caribou run north into a country
that keeps retreating past the horizon,
and I am thinking of you now,
because you never let the earth grieve alone.

*

You knew that terror is also language,
that the lynched body was a sentence
the country wrote and would not read aloud.
You catalogued the smoke, the rope, the postcard
mailed like a receipt for murder—
you did the arithmetic of atrocity
the way Ida B. Wells-Barnett did,
notebook open on the train,
counting the dead into the ledger of the living,
refusing the comfortable lie.

You carried Du Bois inside you like a second spine:
the double consciousness, the veil,
the twoness of a soul that measures itself
by the tape of a world that hates it—
and still you walked into the seminar,
the street, the archive, the church basement,
and taught us how to name the machinery.

*

Now you are gone into the warming dark,
and the animals are going with you,
species by species, a slow procession
out of the only ark we ever had.
You would have said: *these are not separate deaths.*
The floe and the noose, the drought and the ledger—
you traced the single logic underneath,
the ownership of breath, of land, of water,
the deciding of who is permitted to remain.

*

So let the egrets circle where you stood.
Let the bear's last island hold your name.
Let the fever of the earth be read
as the sentence it has always been.

You taught us this, and left us here to speak it:
*America, I have seen your face in the mirror of your enemies,
and it was your own.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tribute poem for Amiri Baraka or a similar revolutionary Black poet, capturing both grief and political rage in the age of climate catastrophe and Trump. Use lowercase throughout and blend nature imagery with critiques of "me-ism," "first-ism," and "rich cowards."
counterfactuals.output:
**for the ones who burned honest**
*(after baraka)*

they buried you in a season the earth forgot how to green,
the rivers running the wrong direction,
the bees leaving no forwarding address.

somewhere a poem is still on fire
and nobody will say your name loud enough
to make the cowards flinch.

you told us
me-ism is a small religion,
a church the size of a mirror,
where the congregation kneels
before its own reflection
and calls the hunger holy.

you told us
first-ism is just a flag
sewn from other people's skin,
america first
me first
mine first
while the ice sheets sign their own obituaries
and the poor learn to swim in their kitchens.

o poet,
they miss you now
in this hour of orange men
and their gold-plated fear,
these rich cowards
who would sell the last clean cloud
for a coupon,
who mistake a fortune for a spine.

look how the maples grieve you,
dropping their green like a language
going quiet.
look how the wind
still tries to read your lines
against the throats of the powerful.

the storms know your rhythm.
the flood remembers your meter.
the drought is just the land
practicing your silence.

so we take up the low sound,
the humming under the boot,
the small fierce thing
that will not go corporate,
will not go quiet,
will not kneel at the mirror.

we say your name
the way you meant it—
not a whisper
but a match,

and the whole rotted house
of first and me and mine
looks up, at last,
afraid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
